newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Germany insists on no EU money for job schemes.
newsitem.headline: Germany insists on no EU money for job schemes.

text.p: Germany turned up the heat on its European Union partners on Sunday, just hours ahead of a two-day EU summit in Amsterdam, by ruling out costly Europe-wide job-creation scheme.
Germany and France, the twin engines behind EU moves towards an ambitious single currency project, are at loggerheads over how to proceed towards monetary union, due to be launched in January, 1999.
The rift between Bonn and Paris, normally a strong alliance at the centre of EU integration, was prompted by this month's socialist victory in French parliamentary elections.
The split threatens to dominate Monday and Tuesday's meeting which was supposed to culminate in agreement on a new treaty setting Europe's course for the next century.

But new French premier Lionel Jospin has told his partners he wants a bigger profile given to creating jobs in the 15-member bloc. He is hostile to the economic austerity required to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU).

France has stunned the Union by demanding more time to study the so-called stability pact, a framework for keeping EU budgets from ballooning into deficit after the planned euro currency is introduced.
Germany vehemently opposes any weakening of the single currency criteria and any job creation schemes which involve pumping huge sums of public cash into grand finance projects.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, architect of the stability pact and a staunch proponent of budgetary discipline, said on Sunday there was no chance Germany would agree to take part in costly job-scheme programmes.
"We will stick to our position that there will be no money flowing from Germany for additional jobs creation programmes," Waigel told Reuters.

"I will not go along with (state job creation programmes) under which Germany pays one third to Europe and gets only 15 percent back," he earlier told the Frankfurter Allgemeine Sonntagszeitung newspaper.
The newspaper cited Waigel as saying he expected some form of agreement on employment strategy at the summit but this would not be tied in with additional spending.

Edmund Stoiber, premier of the southern German state of Bavaria and a well-known euro-sceptic, added to the pressure on EU leaders by calling for the euro to be delayed if stability targets were not met.
In strong language, Stoiber warned politicians they would lose public confidence and harm democracy if they traded the German mark for a soft euro with several start-up members.

"The overriding question for politicians and especially for the public at large is not when the euro will be introduced but rather whether it is a stable euro," Stoiber told Bild am Sonntag newspaper.
"The mark with hard-earned savings attached to it represents the life-time efforts of the people who rebuilt our nation. The mark is inseparately linked to our 'economic miracle'."
"EMU will begin on January 1, 1999 as a stable union or it must be postponed -- and until such a time as the preconditions are in place," Stoiber added.
In Frankfurt, the Bundesbank denied that its president Hans Tietmeyer had urged either a delay of monetary union or a plan to ensure an orderly delay would be possible.
Der Spiegel magazine cited Tietmeyer as having told bankers that a plan was needed to cover the event of a postponement of the euro launch beyond the January 1, 1999 deadline.
But French Finance Minister Dominique Srauss-Kahn, in an advance release of an interview with Germany's ZDF television, hinted that a deal on the stability pact would be forthcoming.
"We might have a text on Sunday evening, but perhaps not. In any case we will find a solution on Monday," ZDF quoted Strauss-Kahn as saying.

EU leaders, due to arrive in the Dutch capital on Sunday evening amid tight security, were expected to agree compromise resolutions underlining the importance of job creation and of coordinating economic policy, attached to the stability pact.
EU finance ministers were to meet to discuss the crisis over dinner (1900 GMT) ahead of the full summit.
